claim: PKM2 is highly expressed in tumour cells and in many proliferative tissues.
source: PKM2 is highly expressed in tumour cells and in many proliferative tissues, and has critical roles in cancer metabolism that remain under intense investigation (Allen and Locasale, 2018; Anastasiou et al., 2011; Christofk et al., 2008a; Dayton et al., 2016), as well as in controlling systemic metabolic homeostasis and inflammation (Palsson-McDermott et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: PKM2 has critical roles in cancer metabolism.
source: PKM2 is highly expressed in tumour cells and in many proliferative tissues, and has critical roles in cancer metabolism that remain under intense investigation (Allen and Locasale, 2018; Anastasiou et al., 2011; Christofk et al., 2008a; Dayton et al., 2016), as well as in controlling systemic metabolic homeostasis and inflammation (Palsson-McDermott et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: PKM2 has roles in controlling systemic metabolic homeostasis and inflammation.
source: PKM2 is highly expressed in tumour cells and in many proliferative tissues, and has critical roles in cancer metabolism that remain under intense investigation (Allen and Locasale, 2018; Anastasiou et al., 2011; Christofk et al., 2008a; Dayton et al., 2016), as well as in controlling systemic metabolic homeostasis and inflammation (Palsson-McDermott et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: PKM2 activity in cancer cells is maintained at a low level by the action of various allosteric ligands or post-translational modifications.
source: In contrast to the highly homologous alternatively spliced variant PKM1, which is thought to be constitutively active, PKM2 activity in cancer cells is maintained at a low level by the action of various allosteric ligands or post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Chaneton and Gottlieb, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Low PKM2 activity promotes pro-tumorigenic functions, including divergence of glucose carbons into biosynthetic and redox-regulating pathways that support proliferation and defence against oxidative stress.
source: Low PKM2 activity promotes pro-tumorigenic functions, including divergence of glucose carbons into biosynthetic and redox-regulating pathways that support proliferation and defence against oxidative stress (Anastasiou et al., 2011; Christofk et al., 2008a; Anastasiou et al., 2012; Lunt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Small-molecule activators that render PKM2 constitutively active attenuate tumour growth.
source: Small-molecule activators, which render PKM2 constitutively active by overcoming endogenous inhibitory cues, attenuate tumour growth, suggesting that regulation of PKM2 activity, rather than increased PKM2 expression per se, is important (Anastasiou et al., 2011; Anastasiou et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017a; Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: FBP binds to a pocket in the C-domain of PKM2.
source: The upstream glycolytic intermediate fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (FBP) binds to a pocket in the C-domain (Dombrauckas et al., 2005) and increases the enzymatic activity of PKM2, thereby establishing a feed-forward loop that prepares lower glycolysis for increased levels of incoming glucose carbons.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: FBP increases the enzymatic activity of PKM2.
source: The upstream glycolytic intermediate fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (FBP) binds to a pocket in the C-domain (Dombrauckas et al., 2005) and increases the enzymatic activity of PKM2, thereby establishing a feed-forward loop that prepares lower glycolysis for increased levels of incoming glucose carbons.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Activation of PKM2 by FBP is associated with a decreased KM for the substrate PEP.
source: Activation of PKM2 by FBP is associated with a decreased KM for the substrate PEP (KMPEP), while the kcat remains unchanged (Chaneton et al., 2012; Boxer et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2010; Yacovan et al., 2012), although some reports also find an elevated kcat (Morgan et al., 2013; Akhtar et al., 2009) and the reason for this discrepancy remains unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Several amino acids regulate PKM2 activity by binding to a pocket in the A domain TIM-barrel core.
source: Additionally, several amino acids regulate PKM2 activity by binding to a pocket in the A domain TIM-barrel core (Chaneton et al., 2012; Yuan et al., 2018; Eigenbrodt et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: L-serine and L-histidine increase PKM2 activity by decreasing KMPEP.
source: L-serine (Ser) and L-histidine (His) increase, whereas L-phenylalanine (Phe), L-alanine (Ala), L-tryptophan (Trp), L-valine (Val) and L-proline (Pro) decrease KMPEP.
evidence: Supported by citations in the preceding sentence

claim: L-phenylalanine, L-alanine, L-tryptophan, L-valine and L-proline decrease PKM2 activity by increasing KMPEP.
source: L-serine (Ser) and L-histidine (His) increase, whereas L-phenylalanine (Phe), L-alanine (Ala), L-tryptophan (Trp), L-valine (Val) and L-proline (Pro) decrease KMPEP.
evidence: Supported by citations in the preceding sentence

claim: FBP promotes PKM2 tetramerisation.
source: FBP promotes, whereas T3 prevents, tetramerisation (Dombrauckas et al., 2005; Morgan et al., 2013; Kato et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: T3 prevents PKM2 tetramerisation.
source: FBP promotes, whereas T3 prevents, tetramerisation (Dombrauckas et al., 2005; Morgan et al., 2013; Kato et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: A PKM2 mutant that cannot bind FBP can still be activated by Ser.
source: A PKM2 mutant that cannot bind FBP can still be activated by Ser and, conversely, a mutant that abolishes Ser binding can be activated by FBP (Chaneton et al., 2012), suggesting that amino acids could work independently from FBP to regulate PKM2.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: A PKM2 mutant that abolishes Ser binding can be activated by FBP.
source: A PKM2 mutant that cannot bind FBP can still be activated by Ser and, conversely, a mutant that abolishes Ser binding can be activated by FBP (Chaneton et al., 2012), suggesting that amino acids could work independently from FBP to regulate PKM2.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Inhibitory amino acids that bind to the same pocket as Ser fail to inhibit PKM2 in the presence of FBP.
source: However, inhibitory amino acids that bind to the same pocket as Ser fail to inhibit the enzyme in the presence of FBP indicating a dominant influence of the latter (Yuan et al., 2018; Sparmann et al., 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: FBP can overcome PKM2 inhibition by T3.
source: Similarly, FBP can overcome PKM2 inhibition by T3 (Kato et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: FBP attenuates, but does not completely prevent, inhibition of PKM2 by Ala.
source: FBP has also been shown to attenuate, but not completely prevent, inhibition of PKM2 by Ala (Ashizawa et al., 1991b).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: The intracellular concentration of FBP in HCT116 cells cultured in RPMI media containing 11 mM glucose is 238.4 ± 67.4 µM.
source: In the presence of high (11 mM) extracellular glucose, [FBP]ic varied between 240–360 µM across the three cell lines (Gluc+, Figure 2A and Table 2)
evidence: Measured using LC-MS as described in methods and shown in Figure 2A and Table 2

claim: The intracellular concentration of FBP in LN229 cells cultured in RPMI media containing 11 mM glucose is 302.0 ± 75.3 µM.
source: In the presence of high (11 mM) extracellular glucose, [FBP]ic varied between 240–360 µM across the three cell lines (Gluc+, Figure 2A and Table 2)
evidence: Measured using LC-MS as described in methods and shown in Figure 2A and Table 2

claim: The intracellular concentration of FBP in SN12C cells cultured in RPMI media containing 11 mM glucose is 355.1 ± 66.2 µM.
source: In the presence of high (11 mM) extracellular glucose, [FBP]ic varied between 240–360 µM across the three cell lines (Gluc+, Figure 2A and Table 2)
evidence: Measured using LC-MS as described in methods and shown in Figure 2A and Table 2

claim: The KDFBP was (25.5 ± 148.1) nM.
source: The KDFBP was (25.5 ± 148.1) nM, after accounting (see Materials and methods) for the amount of co-purified FBP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Measured using fluorescence emission spectroscopy as described in methods and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The upper-limit estimate for the KDFBP from ten replicate binding experiments was 174 nM.
source: Nevertheless, the upper-limit estimate for the KDFBP from ten replicate binding experiments was 174 nM, supporting the idea that FBP is a high-affinity ligand.
evidence: Calculated from ten replicate measurements as described in methods

claim: The KDPhe was (191.0 ± 86.3) µM.
source: The KDPhe and KDSer were (191.0 ± 86.3) µM and (507.5 ± 218.2) µM, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Table 1).
evidence: Measured using microscale thermophoresis as described in methods and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The KDSer was (507.5 ± 218.2) µM.
source: The KDPhe and KDSer were (191.0 ± 86.3) µM and (507.5 ± 218.2) µM, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Table 1).
evidence: Measured using microscale thermophoresis as described in methods and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The calculated fractional saturation of PKM2 with FBP in cells was 0.99.
source: The calculated fractional saturation of PKM2 with FBP was 0.99 (Figure 2B) and remained unchanged even in cells cultured in the absence of glucose (Gluc-), when [FBP]ic decreased to as low as 20 µM.
evidence: Calculated from measured intracellular concentrations and binding affinities as shown in Figure 2B

claim: Addition of exogenous FBP to lysates of HCT116 cells cultured in both Gluc+ and Gluc- media caused little increase in PKM2 activity.
source: Consistent with the prediction of near-saturating PKM2 occupancy by FBP, addition of exogenous FBP to lysates of HCT116 cells cultured in both Gluc+ and Gluc- media caused little increase in PKM2 activity (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: Addition of exogenous Phe to HCT116 lysates resulted in inhibition of PKM2 activity.
source: Addition of exogenous Phe (at physiological intracellular concentrations) to HCT116 lysates resulted in inhibition of PKM2 activity (Figure 2G) and a dose-dependent decrease in kcat/KM (Figure 2H).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 2G and 2H

claim: FBP activated PKM2 in a dose-dependent manner, with an apparent AC50 = (118.1 ± 19.0) nM.
source: FBP activated PKM2 in a dose-dependent manner, with an apparent AC50 = (118.1 ± 19.0) nM (Figure 3A), consistent with the nM binding affinity estimate above.
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 3A

claim: FBP decreased the KMPEP to (0.23 ± 0.04) mM, compared to PKM2apo* [KMPEP = (1.22 ± 0.02) mM].
source: FBP decreased the KMPEP to (0.23 ± 0.04) mM, compared to the absence of any added ligands (PKM2apo*) [KMPEP = (1.22 ± 0.02) mM] (Figure 3B and Table 3).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 3B and Table 3

claim: Addition of Ser resulted in a decrease of the KMPEP to (0.22 ± 0.04) mM.
source: Similarly, addition of Ser resulted in a decrease of the KMPEP to (0.22 ± 0.04) mM, whereas Phe increased the KMPEP to (7.08 ± 1.58) mM.
evidence: Measured experimentally as described in methods

claim: Phe increased the KMPEP to (7.08 ± 1.58) mM.
source: Similarly, addition of Ser resulted in a decrease of the KMPEP to (0.22 ± 0.04) mM, whereas Phe increased the KMPEP to (7.08 ± 1.58) mM.
evidence: Measured experimentally as described in methods

claim: FBP, Phe and Ser act as K-type modulators of PKM2.
source: These results are consistent with previous reports (Dombrauckas et al., 2005; Chaneton et al., 2012; Ikeda and Noguchi, 1998) that FBP, Phe and Ser change the KMPEP but not the kcat and therefore act as K-type modulators (Reinhart, 2004) of PKM2.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citations to published research

claim: In the presence of FBP, addition of Phe resulted in a decrease in the kcat of PKM2 from 349.3 s−1 to 222.3 s−1 (p=0.0075).
source: In the presence of FBP, addition of Phe resulted in a decrease in the kcat of PKM2 from 349.3 s−1 to 222.3 s−1 (p=0.0075), and a simultaneous increase in the KMPEP [(0.65 ± 0.03) mM] compared to PKM2FBP (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: In the presence of FBP, addition of Phe resulted in an increase in the KMPEP to (0.65 ± 0.03) mM compared to PKM2FBP.
source: In the presence of FBP, addition of Phe resulted in a decrease in the kcat of PKM2 from 349.3 s−1 to 222.3 s−1 (p=0.0075), and a simultaneous increase in the KMPEP [(0.65 ± 0.03) mM] compared to PKM2FBP (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: In the absence of FBP, Phe acted as a hyperbolic-specific inhibitor.
source: Further analysis of the kinetic data showed that in the absence of FBP, Phe acted as a hyperbolic-specific (Baici, 2015) inhibitor (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), whereas, with FBP, Phe inhibition of PKM2 changed to a hyperbolic-mixed (Baici, 2015) mechanism (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Inferred from analysis of kinetic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: With FBP, Phe inhibition of PKM2 changed to a hyperbolic-mixed mechanism.
source: Further analysis of the kinetic data showed that in the absence of FBP, Phe acted as a hyperbolic-specific (Baici, 2015) inhibitor (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), whereas, with FBP, Phe inhibition of PKM2 changed to a hyperbolic-mixed (Baici, 2015) mechanism (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Inferred from analysis of kinetic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: Saturating amounts of FBP did not change the measured KDPhe.
source: Phe caused a small but not statistically significant (p=0.150) increase in the binding affinity of FBP (KDFBP) (Figure 3C), and, conversely, saturating amounts of FBP did not change the measured KDPhe (Figure 3D).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 3D

claim: The mass spectrum of PKM2apo* showed a mixture of monomers, dimers and tetramers at an approximate ratio of 1:7:10.
source: The mass spectrum of PKM2apo* showed a mixture of monomers, dimers and tetramers at an approximate ratio of 1:7:10 (Figure 4A,B), with dimers exclusively forming the A-A' dimer assembly, as evidenced from experimental (IM) and theoretical measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured using nESI and IM mass spectrometry as shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: PKM2apo* dimers exclusively form the A-A' dimer assembly.
source: The mass spectrum of PKM2apo* showed a mixture of monomers, dimers and tetramers at an approximate ratio of 1:7:10 (Figure 4A,B), with dimers exclusively forming the A-A' dimer assembly, as evidenced from experimental (IM) and theoretical measurements (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Determined from experimental IM and theoretical measurements as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Addition of exogenous FBP resulted in a decrease in the intensity of monomer and dimer peaks, and a dose-dependent increase in the intensity of the tetramer signal.
source: Addition of exogenous FBP resulted in a decrease in the intensity of monomer and dimer peaks, and a dose-dependent increase in the intensity of the tetramer signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Measured using mass spectrometry as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: PKM2FBP tetramers were more stable than PKM2apo* tetramers with respect to dissociation into dimers and monomers.
source: Furthermore, surface-induced dissociation (SID) experiments revealed that PKM2FBP tetramers were more stable than PKM2apo* tetramers with respect to dissociation into dimers and monomers (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Measured using SID experiments as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Addition of Phe to PKM2apo* caused a decrease in the relative abundance of the tetramers and an increased relative abundance of the dimer species.
source: Addition of Phe to PKM2apo* caused a decrease in the relative abundance of the tetramers and an increased relative abundance of the dimer species (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Measured using mass spectrometry as shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: Phe did not perturb the tetrameric state of PKM2FBP.
source: In contrast, Phe did not perturb the tetrameric state of PKM2FBP (Figure 4A,B), while FBP binding to PKM2Phe resulted in tetramerisation of the protein, indicating that the dominant effect of FBP on PKM2 tetramerisation was unaffected by the order of ligand addition (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Measured using mass spectrometry as shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: FBP binding to PKM2Phe resulted in tetramerisation of the protein.
source: In contrast, Phe did not perturb the tetrameric state of PKM2FBP (Figure 4A,B), while FBP binding to PKM2Phe resulted in tetramerisation of the protein, indicating that the dominant effect of FBP on PKM2 tetramerisation was unaffected by the order of ligand addition (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Measured using mass spectrometry as shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: PKM2 tetramers were found to bind FBP and Phe simultaneously.
source: PKM2 tetramers were found to bind FBP and Phe simultaneously, on the basis of the mass shift resulting from sequential addition of either ligand alone or in combination (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inferred from mass shift measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: FBP caused subtle conformational changes in the PKM2 tetramer, evidenced by a modest decrease in the DTCCSHe between 9500 Å2–9650 Å2.
source: Additionally, differences in the collision cross section (DTCCSHe) distribution, which reflects the conformational heterogeneity of proteins, suggested that FBP caused subtle conformational changes in the tetramer, evidenced by a modest decrease in the DTCCSHe between 9500 Å2–9650 Å2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Measured using IM-MS as shown in Figure 4D

claim: The addition of Phe partially reversed the changed DTCCSHe to a distribution closely resembling that of PKM2apo*.
source: The addition of Phe partially reversed the changed DTCCSHe to a distribution closely resembling that of PKM2apo* (Figure 4D).
evidence: Measured using IM-MS as shown in Figure 4D

claim: In the presence of Phe, half-stoichiometric amounts of FBP were sufficient to induce tetramerisation with slow kinetics [ktet = (812.5 s ± 284.6 s−1)].
source: Moreover, in the presence of Phe, half-stoichiometric amounts of FBP were sufficient to induce tetramerisation with slow kinetics [ktet = (812.5 s ± 284.6 s−1)], whereas equivalent half-stoichiometric amounts of FBP in the absence of Phe were unable to fully convert PKM2 monomers and dimers into tetramers (Figure 4E).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 4E

claim: The inhibitory effect of Phe on the ability of FBP to enhance PKM2 activity is not due to Phe preventing FBP-induced tetramerisation.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the inhibitory effect of Phe on the ability of FBP to enhance PKM2 activity is not due to Phe preventing FBP-induced tetramerisation and suggest it is likely due to interference with the allosteric communication between the FBP and the active site.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing Phe does not prevent FBP-induced tetramerisation but still inhibits activity

claim: Analyses of protein volume and solvent accessibility of the MD trajectories found no evidence of large global protein conformational changes induced by FBP.
source: Subsequent analyses of protein volume and solvent accessibility of the trajectories (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), found no evidence of large global protein conformational changes induced by FBP, consistent with the modest DTCCSHe changes we observed by IM-MS (Figure 4D).
evidence: Analyzed from MD simulations as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Backbone correlations extracted from the sub-states separated into two clusters (C1 and C2) that were dominated by sub-states from PKM2apo and PKM2FBP simulations, respectively.
source: Backbone correlations extracted from the sub-states separated into two clusters (C1 and C2) that were dominated by sub-states from PKM2apo and PKM2FBP simulations, respectively, in addition to cluster C3 that was populated by sub-states from both simulations (Figure 5B).
evidence: Analyzed using AlloHubMat from MD simulations as shown in Figure 5B

claim: The strength of the coupling signal between the AlloHubFs correlated with the positional entropy.
source: We found that the strength of the coupling signal between the AlloHubFs correlated with the positional entropy (Figure 5D), corroborating the idea that local backbone flexibility contributed to the transmission of allosteric information.
evidence: Analyzed from MD simulations as shown in Figure 5D

claim: All AlloHubFs, with the exception of Hub5 and Hub6, coincided with minimal distance pathways between the FBP binding pocket and the active site.
source: Remarkably, all AlloHubFs, with the exception of Hub5 and Hub6, coincided with minimal distance pathways (Dijkstra, 1959) between the FBP binding pocket and the active site (Figure 5E).
evidence: Analyzed from MD simulations as shown in Figure 5E

claim: The KDFBP for all AlloHubMs were similar to PKM2(WT), with the exception of PKM2(R489L), which bound to FBP with low affinity.
source: Importantly, the KDFBP for all AlloHubMs were similar to PKM2(WT), with the exception of PKM2(R489L), which bound to FBP with low affinity (Figure 6—figure supplement 4 and Table 7).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4 and Table 7

claim: PKM2 AlloHubMs I124G, F244V, K305Q, F307P and R489L showed attenuated activation by FBP.
source: PKM2 AlloHubMs I124G, F244V, K305Q, F307P and R489L showed attenuated activation by FBP (Figure 6B) indicating that AlloHubMat successfully identified residues that mediate the allosteric effect of FBP.
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 6B

claim: Phe addition significantly hindered FBP-induced activation in I124G, F244V, and R489L.
source: Similar to PKM2(WT), Phe addition significantly hindered FBP-induced activation in I124G, F244V, and R489L (Figure 6C).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 6C

claim: K305Q and F307P were allosterically inert, with no detectable response in activity upon addition of either FBP or Phe.
source: In contrast, K305Q and F307P were allosterically inert, with no detectable response in activity upon addition of either FBP or Phe (Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 5

claim: PKM2(F307P) had a KMPEP similar to that of PKM2(WT)FBP, indicating that this mutant displays a constitutively high substrate affinity.
source: While for PKM2(K305Q) this outcome could be explained by very low basal activity, PKM2(F307P) had a KMPEP similar to that of PKM2(WT)FBP, indicating that this mutant displays a constitutively high substrate affinity (Figure 6—figure supplement 5 and Table 8).
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5 and Table 8

claim: PKM2(A327S) and PKM2(C358A) retained intact activation by FBP.
source: Intriguingly, two AlloHubMs, PKM2(A327S) and PKM2(C358A), retained intact activation by FBP (Figure 6B), suggesting either that the amino acid substitutions were functionally neutral or that these residues are not required for FBP-induced activation.
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 6B

claim: Addition of Phe failed to attenuate FBP-induced activation of PKM2(A327S) and PKM2(C358A).
source: However, addition of Phe failed to attenuate FBP-induced activation of these AlloHubMs (Figure 6C), indicating that residues A327 and C358 have a role in coupling the allosteric effect of Phe with that of FBP.
evidence: Measured experimentally as shown in Figure 6C

claim: Residues A327 and C358 have a role in coupling the allosteric effect of Phe with that of FBP.
source: However, addition of Phe failed to attenuate FBP-induced activation of these AlloHubMs (Figure 6C), indicating that residues A327 and C358 have a role in coupling the allosteric effect of Phe with that of FBP.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing these mutants retain FBP activation but lose Phe inhibition

claim: FBP-induced dynamic coupling between distal residues functions, in part, to enable Phe to interfere with FBP-induced allostery.
source: Our work shows that FBP-induced dynamic coupling between distal residues functions, in part, to enable Phe to interfere with FBP-induced allostery.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental and computational results

claim: AlloHubMat successfully identified residues involved in FBP-induced allosteric activation of PKM2.
source: In summary, evaluation of the allosteric properties of AlloHubMs demonstrated that AlloHubMat successfully identified residues involved in FBP-induced allosteric activation of PKM2.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental validation of computationally predicted residues

claim: Enzymatic activation of PKM2 can be uncoupled from tetramerisation.
source: Therefore, beyond its immediate goals, our study has broader implications for understanding the regulation of PKM2 as it suggests that enzymatic activation can be uncoupled from tetramerisation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing mutants that tetramerize but are not activated, and vice versa
